rv.q: Jan’s quick-change resets are a joy to behold and, thanks to illusionist Paul Kieve, Vernel, or parts of him, often seem to be in two places at once.
Instructions for Correct Assembly begins by advertising its cleverness – and goes on to be far cleverer and more penetrating.
It is deftly done and is both funny and, at times, heart-achingly sad.
If the script finally runs out of battery, this is a lively new play bustling with ideas and laughs.
The grief, though, to my mind is not as well handled.
The meandering script has an error that any competent producer ought to spot: a lack of conflict between the parents.
Instructions for Correct Assembly is an interesting and inventive piece of theatre.
Thomas Eccleshare has written an amusing Sci-Fi satire on parental expectation and parental disappointment.
Instructions For Correct Assembly is never quite as alarming as it should be.
This is an enjoyably cartoon critique of everyday conformity, but don’t expect anything else.

cn.t: Critics mostly praise this clever sci-fi satire about parents assembling a replacement child, applauding its strong cast and striking design, though some find the premise derivative and underdeveloped beyond its initial concept.
